full_text:
Bakhtiyar related the story of King Dadbin of ancient Persia:

'King Dadbin had two ministers: the first was Kardan, an unprincipled courtier who used his office to amass gold, sell justice to the wealthy, and flatter the king’s vanity; the second was Rast-Rushan, an upright statesman whose name meant "Righteous Light," who spent his energy building public granaries, protecting the peasantry, and refusing all bribes.

Kardan, envious of Rast-Rushan’s spotless reputation, forged letters to convince the king that Rast-Rushan was secretly plotting with foreign enemies.

King Dadbin, desiring to discover the truth himself, donned the disguise of a common dervish and spent a month wandering through the provinces of his empire.

Wherever he went, the farmers, merchants, and scholars cursed the name of Kardan, recounting his extortions and cruelties; while everywhere, the people blessed Rast-Rushan with tears of gratitude, showing the schools, irrigation canals, and fair markets he had established!

The king returned to his capital, cast off his disguise, and held a public tribunal.

He confronted Kardan with the evidence of his extortions, stripped him of his robes, and banished him to the salt mines; while Rast-Rushan was appointed Grand Vizier with supreme authority over the empire.

King Dadbin proclaimed: "The flatterer brought me letters of false praise, but the people’s bread testified to the truth! Righteousness is the only foundation that sustains the state."'
moral: Integrity that serves the public good outlasts the deceitful conspiracies of corrupt ministers.
